title: Carl Sagan: American Hero
summary: Hosts Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant profile astronomer and science communicator Carl Sagan: his childhood in Brooklyn and New Jersey, the 1939 World's Fair that sparked his interest in science, his degrees and Cornell career, NASA consulting and the Voyager Golden Record, scientific ideas such as the greenhouse effect and the faint young Sun paradox, his public image and criticism from the scientific establishment, his skepticism and agnosticism, the nuclear winter Parade magazine controversy, Cosmos (1980 PBS series), Contact, his illness and death at 62-64 range, and his archive sold to the Library of Congress. Includes listener mail from Connie about anatomy and anxiety and a shout-out to her brother Matt.

segments.title: Opening banter and Sagan as explainer
segments.summary: Hosts chat about their late nights, then introduce Carl Sagan as a creative science communicator and explainer, a generalist, and a forerunner of their own show; they compare him to Neil deGrasse Tyson, Brian Greene and Bill Nye.

segments.title: Sagan's public image, billions and billions, and cannabis essay
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Sagan's popularity and criticism from scientists, his 'billions and billions' catchphrase (which he said he never actually said on Carson), and his essay 'Marijuana Reconsidered' praising cannabis for improving his appreciation of art.

segments.title: Childhood, family and high school
segments.summary: Sagan's birth in Brooklyn to a Ukrainian immigrant father and a mother described as overbearing with high expectations. He moved to New Jersey and was voted class brain at Rahway High School; his 1953 questionnaire self-ratings are discussed.

segments.title: Sagan archive and Seth MacFarland donation
segments.summary: Sagan's papers, including 798 boxes, were sold to the Library of Congress by his widow Ann Druyan, with funds from Seth MacFarland, who named the collection after Sagan and Druyan. The hosts note Sagan dictated his writing into a dictaphone.

segments.title: 1939 World's Fair and the mid-century science boom
segments.summary: Sagan's visit to the 1939 New York World's Fair at age five sparked his interest in science. The hosts discuss the optimism about science from the late 1930s through the 1970s and the technological plateau since then. They describe Sagan as a nuanced skeptic open to discussion, and his 1969 UFO conference where all sides spoke.

segments.title: Listener email about dogmatism
segments.summary: The hosts say they received an email calling it dangerous to mention other schools of thought, and reply that presenting multiple viewpoints is healthy discussion, citing their crop circle episode.

segments.title: Academic career, NASA consulting and Voyager Golden Record
segments.summary: Sagan earned degrees in physics and a doctorate in astronomy, had a short stint at Harvard before moving to Cornell, where he set up the Laboratory for Planetary Studies. He consulted for NASA and pushed it toward humanities, including the Voyager Golden Records with images, sounds, and Ann Druyan's brainwave-based music.

segments.title: Greenhouse effect, faint young Sun paradox, Titan, and criticism
segments.summary: Sagan's work on Venus and the greenhouse effect, the faint young Sun paradox with George Mullen, and his claim about organic molecules on Titan are covered. The hosts discuss the scientific community's unwritten rule against speculating outside one's expertise, and his frequent TV appearances including Carson and Parade Magazine.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Brief closing remarks and show information, including the hosts' website and social channels.
